name: Synthetic Portraiture
title: Synthetic Portraiture
answer: Synthetic portraiture is the making of human or human-like likenesses with generative models rather than a camera and a sitting subject. It sits inside photography and hyper-realism, where the finished picture is judged by the same standards as a photograph: light, skin, pose, lens behaviour, and the small imperfections that make a face read as real. The subject covers everything from a single generated headshot to full editorial series, character sheets for film and games, and the deliberate blurring of the line between captured and computed images. It also covers the reverse question, which is how a viewer or an editor can tell which side of that line a picture came from.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on diffusion models and, in some pipelines, generative adversarial networks, usually accessed through hosted services or run locally on a consumer or workstation GPU. Text prompts set the broad brief, while control inputs such as pose skeletons, depth maps, and reference images hold the composition steady across a set. Upscaling and face-restoration passes add resolution and skin detail after the first generation, and a colour-managed viewer or editing application is used to grade the result. Storage and naming discipline matter more than in ordinary photography, because a single portrait can pass through many intermediate files before it is finished.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical session starts with a written brief and a set of reference photographs for lighting, wardrobe, and expression, then moves to prompt and seed exploration until a usable base image appears. The maker then iterates with inpainting, outpainting, and control inputs to fix hands, hair, eyes, and background, often compositing generated elements onto a real or generated plate. Retouching follows the habits of commercial photography: dodge and burn, frequency separation, and grain, with the aim of removing the tell-tale smoothness that marks an untouched generation. Consistency across a series is the hard part, and it is usually solved with fixed seeds, trained likenesses, or reference-driven workflows rather than by luck.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights around synthetic portraits are unsettled, and the practical questions are consent, likeness, and disclosure. A generated face may resemble a real person by accident, and a model trained on photographs of real people raises questions about whose face and whose labour sit inside the output. Publishers, agencies, and platforms increasingly expect a label or a note in the caption when an image is generated or materially altered, and some outlets refuse such images in news contexts altogether. Provenance tools that attach signed metadata to a file are one response, though they only help when the chain is kept intact. Anyone working commercially should treat model licences, training-data terms, and local publicity rules as things to check rather than assume.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration with real capture: generated elements placed into photographed scenes, real faces relit and extended with models, and camera or editing software offering synthesis as a routine step. Detection and provenance are advancing alongside generation, so the argument over what counts as a photograph is likely to be settled by disclosure norms rather than by technical proof. Demand is growing for consistent synthetic characters that can be reused across campaigns and productions, which pushes the field toward trained, identity-stable models rather than one-off prompts. For photographers, the durable skills look like the old ones: lighting, direction, taste, and the judgement to know when a computed face is the right answer and when it is not.
